::: {.box}
These notes follow Chapter 1 of Lawvere–Rosebrugh, *Sets for Mathematics*.
Numbers such as "Definition 1.14" or "Exercise 1.15" refer to the book. In the
exercises taken from §§1.5–1.8 (1.15–1.28), argue *only* from the axioms and
definitions stated here, plus ordinary logic; do not appeal to what you know
about sets from $\ZFC$. In Exercise 1.30 you work in ordinary mathematics, to
see how much of the structure of abstract sets is shared by other familiar
categories. When an exercise is a statement, prove the statement.
:::

## Sets as a category

In $\ZFC$ the primitive notion is **membership**: a set is determined by its
elements, and everything else (pairs, functions, …) is coded by membership. In
Lawvere's approach the primitive notions are **sets** and **mappings** between
them, together with **composition** of mappings. An *abstract set* has no
internal structure beyond the fact that its elements can be told apart;
everything we want to say about a set must be expressed through the mappings
into and out of it. Even "element" becomes a derived notion: an element of $A$
is a particular kind of mapping *into* $A$.

## Categories

::: {#def-category}
## Category (L–R, Definition 1.13)

A **category** $\Cat$ has the following data:

- **Objects**, denoted $A, B, C, \dots$
- **Arrows**, denoted $f, g, h, \dots$ (also called *morphisms* or *maps*).
- To each arrow $f$ is assigned an object $\dom(f)$, its **domain**, and an
  object $\cod(f)$, its **codomain**. If $\dom(f) = A$ and $\cod(f) = B$ we
  write $f \colon A \to B$ or $A \xrightarrow{\;f\;} B$.
- **Composition:** to each pair $f \colon A \to B$ and $g \colon B \to C$ is
  assigned an arrow $gf \colon A \to C$, called "the composite $g$ following
  $f$" (also written $g \circ f$).
- **Identities:** to each object $A$ is assigned an arrow
  $\id{A} \colon A \to A$, called "the identity on $A$".

These data satisfy the axioms

- **Associativity:** if
  $A \xrightarrow{\;f\;} B \xrightarrow{\;g\;} C \xrightarrow{\;h\;} D$, then
  $h(gf) = (hg)f$;
- **Identity:** if $f \colon A \to B$, then $f = f\,\id{A}$ and
  $f = \id{B}\,f$.
:::

Note that $gf$ is only defined when the codomain of $f$ is *exactly* the domain
of $g$. A diagram of objects and arrows is **commutative** if any two paths of
arrows with the same start and end have equal composites; for example, the
triangle formed by $f \colon A \to B$, $g \colon B \to C$ and
$m \colon A \to C$ commutes precisely when $m = gf$.

::: {#def-isomorphism}
## Isomorphism

Objects $A$ and $B$ of a category are **isomorphic**, written $A \cong B$, if
there are arrows $f \colon A \to B$ and $g \colon B \to A$ with
$gf = \id{A}$ and $fg = \id{B}$. Such an $f$ is an **isomorphism**.
:::

::: {#def-terminal-initial}
## Terminal and initial objects

An object $T$ of a category $\Cat$ is **terminal** if for every object $A$ of
$\Cat$ there is exactly one arrow $A \to T$. An object $I$ is **initial** if
for every object $A$ there is exactly one arrow $I \to A$.
:::

::: {#rem-terminal-initial}
The book introduces "terminal" and "initial" only for the category of sets
(see the axioms below), but the definitions make sense in any category, and
that is how they are used in @exr-LR-1-30.
:::

## The axioms of Chapter 1

We write $\Set$ for the category of abstract sets and (arbitrary) mappings.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Axiom: $\Set$ is a category

Abstract sets and mappings form a category, whose objects are called **sets**
and whose arrows are called **mappings**.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Axiom: Terminal set

There is a set $\one$ such that for any set $A$ there is exactly one mapping
$A \to \one$.
:::

The book gives this unique mapping the same name $A$ as its domain; to avoid
confusion we write it $\term{A} \colon A \to \one$. In a given discussion
$\one$ denotes a *chosen* terminal set (by @exr-LR-1-28 (b) the choice makes no
difference).

::: {#def-element}
## Element (L–R, Definition 1.3)

An **element** of a set $A$ is any mapping whose codomain is $A$ and whose
domain is $\one$, i.e. any $a \colon \one \to A$.
:::

Thus *element is a special case of mapping*, and *evaluation is a special
case of composition*: if $f \colon A \to B$ and $a \colon \one \to A$, then
$fa \colon \one \to B$ is an element of $B$, and we define the **value** of
$f$ at $a$ by $f(a) := fa$. Associativity then gives $(gf)(a) = g(f(a))$.

::: {#def-generalized-element}
## Generalized element (L–R, §1.6)

A **generalized element** of $A$ (or *variable element of $A$ varying over
$T$*) is an arbitrary mapping $x \colon T \to A$ with codomain $A$; its domain
$T$ need not be $\one$.
:::

::: {#def-separator}
## Separator (L–R, Definition 1.14)

An object $S$ in a category $\Cat$ is a **separator** if and only if whenever
$f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y$ are arrows of $\Cat$ with the same domain and the
same codomain, then
$$
\bigl(\forall x\, [\, x \colon S \to X \;\Rightarrow\; f_1 x = f_2 x \,]\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; f_1 = f_2 .
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Axiom: The terminal object $\one$ separates mappings in $\Set$

A one-element set $\one$ is a separator in $\Set$; that is, if
$f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y$, then
$$
\bigl(\forall x\, [\, x \colon \one \to X \;\Rightarrow\; f_1 x = f_2 x \,]\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; f_1 = f_2 .
$$
:::

In words: two mappings with the same domain and codomain that have the same
value at every element are equal. Contrapositively, if $f_1 \neq f_2$ there is
an element $x$ of $X$ with $f_1(x) \neq f_2(x)$.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Axiom: Initial set

There is a set $\zero$ such that for any set $A$ there is exactly one mapping
$\zero \to A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Axiom: Nondegeneracy of $\Set$

$$
\zero \not\cong \one .
$$
:::

::: {#def-coseparator}
## Coseparator (L–R, Definition 1.19)

An object $V$ of a category $\Cat$ is a **coseparator** if for any $A$ and any
parallel pair $a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A$ (of generalized elements of $A$),
$$
\bigl(\forall \varphi\, [\, \varphi \colon A \to V \;\Rightarrow\;
\varphi a_0 = \varphi a_1 \,]\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; a_0 = a_1 .
$$
Equivalently: if $a_0 \neq a_1$, then there is some $\varphi \colon A \to V$
with $\varphi a_0 \neq \varphi a_1$. We say that $V$ **can discriminate
elements** if this condition holds for $T = \one$.
:::

A mapping $\varphi \colon A \to V$ is thought of as a ($V$-valued) *property*
of the elements of $A$, so a coseparator is an object of values with enough
properties to tell elements apart.

::: {#rem-two}
## The set $\two$ (L–R, §1.7)

The book provisionally assumes a set $\two$ with exactly two elements
$0, 1 \colon \one \to \two$ (made precise by the axioms of Chapter 2) and
claims (Claim 1.21) that $\two$ is a coseparator in $\Set$. None of the
exercises below depend on this.
:::

## Exercises

Two consequences of the axioms *Terminal set* and *Initial set* are used again
and again below:

::: {.callout-tip}
## A recurring observation

The only mapping $\one \to \one$ is $\id{\one}$, and the only mapping
$\zero \to \zero$ is $\id{\zero}$. More generally, any two arrows *into* a
terminal object with the same domain are equal, and any two arrows *out of*
an initial object with the same codomain are equal.
:::

### Separators

::: {#exr-LR-1-15}
## L–R 1.15

In the category of abstract sets $\Set$, any set $A$ with at least one element
$x_0 \colon \one \to A$ is also a separator.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Let $f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y$ and suppose that $f_1 a = f_2 a$ for every
$a \colon A \to X$. We must show $f_1 = f_2$. Since $\one$ is a separator
(axiom), it suffices to show $f_1 x = f_2 x$ for every element
$x \colon \one \to X$.

So fix $x \colon \one \to X$ and consider the generalized element
$$
a := x\,\term{A} \colon A \xrightarrow{\;\term{A}\;} \one \xrightarrow{\;x\;} X ,
$$
the *constant* map with value $x$. By hypothesis $f_1 a = f_2 a$, i.e.
$f_1 (x\,\term{A}) = f_2 (x\,\term{A})$. Composing on the right with the given
element $x_0 \colon \one \to A$ and using associativity,
$$
f_1\, x\, (\term{A}\, x_0) \;=\; f_2\, x\, (\term{A}\, x_0).
$$
Now $\term{A} x_0 \colon \one \to \one$, and the only mapping $\one \to \one$
is $\id{\one}$. Hence $\term{A} x_0 = \id{\one}$, and by the identity law
$f_1 x = f_2 x$. As $x$ was arbitrary, $f_1 = f_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Remarks

The key idea is to turn an element $x$ of $X$ into a generalized element
$A \to X$ by making it constant, and then to recover $x$ by evaluating at the
element $x_0$ of $A$. Without $x_0$ we could not cancel $\term{A}$, and
@exr-LR-1-16 shows that the hypothesis cannot be dropped.
:::

::: {#exr-LR-1-16}
## L–R 1.16

In the category of abstract sets $\Set$ the initial set $\zero$ is not a
separator. (Assume that two sets $A$ and $B$ exist with at least two maps
$A \to B$.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

By assumption there are $f_1, f_2 \colon A \to B$ with $f_1 \neq f_2$. For
$\zero$ to be a separator we would need: if $f_1 x = f_2 x$ for every
$x \colon \zero \to A$, then $f_1 = f_2$. But for any $x \colon \zero \to A$,
both $f_1 x$ and $f_2 x$ are mappings $\zero \to B$, and by the axiom *Initial
set* there is exactly one such mapping. Hence $f_1 x = f_2 x$ for all
$x \colon \zero \to A$, while $f_1 \neq f_2$. So $\zero$ is not a separator.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Remarks

*Why is the extra assumption needed?* The axioms of Chapter 1 alone do not
guarantee two distinct parallel mappings. Consider the category with two
objects $\zero, \one$ and only three arrows: $\id{\zero}$, $\id{\one}$, and one
arrow $u \colon \zero \to \one$ (composition is forced). In it $\one$ is
terminal, $\zero$ is initial, every hom-set has at most one element (so
*every* object, including $\zero$, is a separator, and in particular $\one$
separates), and $\zero \not\cong \one$ because there is no arrow
$\one \to \zero$. So all the axioms of Chapter 1 hold, yet $\zero$ is a
separator. This is a first example of a *model* of a fragment of the
categorical axioms, much like the small models of fragments of $\ZFC$ we
studied earlier.

Once the set $\two$ with elements $0 \neq 1 \colon \one \to \two$ is available
(Chapter 2), one can take $A = \one$, $B = \two$.

Compare with @exr-LR-1-15: $\zero$ fails precisely because it has no elements
(@exr-LR-1-18).
:::

### The empty set

::: {#exr-LR-1-18}
## L–R 1.18

How many mappings are there from $\zero$ to $\one$? From $\zero$ to $\zero$?
From $\one$ to $\zero$? (And so how many elements does $\zero$ have?)

*Hint:* To answer the third question requires more axioms than do the other
two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

*From $\zero$ to $\one$: exactly one.* This follows from *Initial set* (with
$A = \one$), and equally from *Terminal set* (with $A = \zero$). Call it
$u \colon \zero \to \one$.

*From $\zero$ to $\zero$: exactly one,* by *Initial set* with $A = \zero$.
Since $\id{\zero}$ is such a mapping, it is $\id{\zero}$.

*From $\one$ to $\zero$: none.* Suppose, for a contradiction, that
$x \colon \one \to \zero$. Then

- $u x \colon \one \to \one$, so $u x = \id{\one}$ (Terminal set);
- $x u \colon \zero \to \zero$, so $x u = \id{\zero}$ (Initial set).

Thus $x$ and $u$ are mutually inverse and $\zero \cong \one$, contradicting
*Nondegeneracy*. Hence there is no mapping $\one \to \zero$.

Since elements of $\zero$ are by definition mappings $\one \to \zero$,
**$\zero$ has no elements**: it is an empty set, which justifies the name.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Remarks

- The first two answers use one axiom each; the third uses *Terminal set*,
  *Initial set*, and *Nondegeneracy*.
- The argument shows that, given the other axioms, Nondegeneracy is
  *equivalent* to the apparently stronger statement "there is no mapping
  $\one \to \zero$". The converse is immediate: an isomorphism
  $\zero \cong \one$ includes a mapping $\one \to \zero$.
- *Extension.* If there is any mapping $h \colon A \to \zero$, then
  $A \cong \zero$. With $e \colon \zero \to A$ the unique map, $he = \id{\zero}$
  by initiality. For $eh = \id{A}$ one needs one more axiom: $A$ has no
  elements (an element $a$ would give an element $ha$ of $\zero$), so $eh$ and
  $\id{A}$ agree at every element vacuously, and they are equal because $\one$
  separates mappings.
- Contrast with $\ZFC$: there, $\emptyset$ has no elements by definition, and
  is unique by Extensionality. Here, the emptiness of $\zero$ is a *theorem*
  about mappings, derived from a property (initiality) that does not mention
  elements at all.
:::

### Coseparators

::: {#exr-LR-1-20}
## L–R 1.20

Use the fact that $\one$ is a separator in the category of abstract sets to
show that (in that category), if $V$ can discriminate elements, then it can
discriminate generalized elements. Thus, in $\Set$ the general $T$ in
@def-coseparator could safely be replaced by $T = \one$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

Assume $V$ discriminates elements: for every set $A$ and all
$b_0, b_1 \colon \one \to A$,
$$
\bigl(\forall \varphi \colon A \to V,\ \varphi b_0 = \varphi b_1\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\; b_0 = b_1 . \tag{*}
$$
Let $a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A$ be generalized elements such that
$\varphi a_0 = \varphi a_1$ for every $\varphi \colon A \to V$. We show
$a_0 = a_1$. Because $\one$ separates mappings, it suffices to show
$a_0 t = a_1 t$ for every element $t \colon \one \to T$.

Fix $t \colon \one \to T$. Then $a_0 t$ and $a_1 t$ are elements of $A$, and
for every $\varphi \colon A \to V$, by associativity,
$$
\varphi (a_0 t) = (\varphi a_0) t = (\varphi a_1) t = \varphi (a_1 t).
$$
By $(*)$, $a_0 t = a_1 t$. Since $t$ was arbitrary, $a_0 = a_1$.

The converse (discriminating generalized elements implies discriminating
elements) is trivial, since elements are generalized elements with
$T = \one$. So in $\Set$ the two conditions are equivalent.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Remarks

- Before starting, write out exactly what must be shown: there are two layers
  of quantifiers (over $t$ and over $\varphi$). Note that $(*)$ cannot be
  applied directly to $a_0, a_1$, which are not elements.
- Associativity does all the work: "evaluate first, then apply $\varphi$"
  equals "apply $\varphi$, then evaluate".
- This is the dual of the role of the separator: $\one$ lets us reduce
  statements about generalized elements to statements about ordinary
  elements. In categories where $\one$ is not a separator (e.g. groups or
  vector spaces, see @exr-LR-1-30) the reduction fails, which is why
  @def-coseparator is stated for general $T$.
:::

### Uniqueness properties

::: {#exr-LR-1-28}
## L–R 1.28

(a) Show that identity arrows in a category are unique, i.e. if
    $\id{A} \colon A \to A$ and $\id{A}' \colon A \to A$ both satisfy the
    equations for identity arrows, then $\id{A} = \id{A}'$.
(b) Show that the set $\one$ is unique "up to unique isomorphism", i.e. if
    $\one'$ also satisfies the axiom of the terminal set, then there are
    unique mappings $f \colon \one \to \one'$ and $g \colon \one' \to \one$,
    and that $gf = \id{\one}$ and $fg = \id{\one'}$.
(c) Similarly, show that the empty set $\zero$ is unique up to unique
    isomorphism.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

**(a)** The identity equations say: $h\,\id{A} = h$ for every
$h \colon A \to B$, and $\id{A}\,k = k$ for every $k \colon C \to A$; likewise
for $\id{A}'$. Consider the composite $\id{A}\,\id{A}'$. Using that $\id{A}'$
is a right identity, with $h = \id{A}$, we get $\id{A}\,\id{A}' = \id{A}$.
Using that $\id{A}$ is a left identity, with $k = \id{A}'$, we get
$\id{A}\,\id{A}' = \id{A}'$. Hence
$$
\id{A} = \id{A}\,\id{A}' = \id{A}' .
$$

**(b)** Since $\one'$ satisfies the terminal set axiom, there is exactly one
mapping $f \colon \one \to \one'$; since $\one$ does, there is exactly one
mapping $g \colon \one' \to \one$. Now $gf \colon \one \to \one$, and the only
mapping $\one \to \one$ is $\id{\one}$; so $gf = \id{\one}$. Symmetrically,
$fg \colon \one' \to \one'$ and the only such mapping is $\id{\one'}$, so
$fg = \id{\one'}$. Thus $\one \cong \one'$. The isomorphism is *unique*: any
isomorphism $\one \to \one'$ is in particular a mapping $\one \to \one'$,
hence equals $f$.

**(c)** Dually, let $\zero'$ also satisfy the initial set axiom. There is
exactly one $f \colon \zero \to \zero'$ (initiality of $\zero$) and exactly
one $g \colon \zero' \to \zero$ (initiality of $\zero'$). Then
$gf \colon \zero \to \zero$ must equal $\id{\zero}$, the only mapping
$\zero \to \zero$, and $fg \colon \zero' \to \zero'$ must equal $\id{\zero'}$.
So $f$ is an isomorphism, and it is the only one, since it is the only mapping
$\zero \to \zero'$ at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Remarks

- The proofs use nothing specific to $\Set$: in *any* category, identities are
  unique and terminal (initial) objects are unique up to unique isomorphism.
  This is what justifies speaking of "the" terminal set: any statement about
  it is insensitive to which terminal set was chosen.
- In (a), only "$\id{A}'$ is a right identity" and "$\id{A}$ is a left
  identity" are used, exactly as for identity elements of a monoid.
- In (b), both composites must be checked; one-sided inverses do not make an
  isomorphism.
- Compare with $\ZFC$: $\emptyset$ is *literally* unique by Extensionality,
  while $\{\emptyset\}$, $\{\{\emptyset\}\}$, and $\{7\}$ are all different
  one-element sets. In the categorical approach these are indistinguishable:
  the theory only ever pins objects down up to (unique) isomorphism.
:::

### Categories of structures

::: {#exr-LR-1-30}
## L–R 1.30

(a) Show that (finite-dimensional) vector spaces as objects and linear
    transformations as arrows form a category with composition of arrows
    defined by composition of mappings. Show that a one-dimensional space $S$
    is a separator; is it a coseparator? Is the terminal object a separator?
(b) Show that groups as objects and group homomorphisms as arrows form a
    category with composition of arrows defined by composition of mappings.
    Show that the additive group of integers is a separator.
(c) Show that partially ordered sets as objects and monotone
    (= order-preserving) mappings as arrows form a category with composition
    of arrows defined by composition of mappings. Is the terminal object a
    separator in this category? Is there a coseparator?
(d) A **finite state machine** with two inputs $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is a
    finite set $Q$ of "states" and a pair of endomaps
    $\alpha, \beta \colon Q \to Q$ that effect the elementary state
    transitions of which the machine is capable. Given another such machine
    with state set $Q'$, a **homomorphism** is a mapping
    $\varphi \colon Q \to Q'$ of state sets preserving the transitions in the
    sense that
    $$
    \varphi\alpha = \alpha'\varphi \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \varphi\beta = \beta'\varphi ,
    $$
    where $\alpha', \beta' \colon Q' \to Q'$ denote the corresponding state
    transitions of the second machine. Define composition of homomorphisms and
    show that a category results.
:::

In parts (a)–(c), "separator", "coseparator" and "terminal object" are meant
in the sense of @def-separator, @def-coseparator and @def-terminal-initial,
applied to the category at hand. In particular, the "elements"
$x \colon S \to X$ that a separator $S$ uses to test arrows are arrows *of that
category* (linear maps, homomorphisms, monotone maps), not arbitrary
functions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution: a remark common to (a)–(d)

In each case the arrows are certain mappings between underlying sets,
composition is composition of mappings, and the identity arrow on an object is
the identity mapping of its underlying set. Therefore, once we know that

(i) the identity mapping is an arrow, and
(ii) the composite of two arrows is again an arrow,

the associativity and identity laws hold automatically, because they hold for
mappings in $\Set$. So in each part the only real work in "show that a
category results" is checking (i) and (ii). Strictly speaking an arrow should
be recorded as the triple (domain, codomain, underlying mapping), since the
same function can be an arrow between different structures on the same
underlying sets; nothing below depends on this.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to (a): vector spaces

Fix a field $k$ and consider finite-dimensional vector spaces over $k$ with
linear maps.

*Category.* The identity map is linear. If $f \colon U \to V$ and
$g \colon V \to W$ are linear then
$gf(\lambda u + \mu u') = g(\lambda f u + \mu f u') = \lambda\, gf u + \mu\, gf u'$,
so $gf$ is linear.

*A one-dimensional space $S$ is a separator.* Fix a nonzero $s \in S$, so
$S = \{\lambda s : \lambda \in k\}$. For every vector $v$ in a space $X$ the
map $x_v \colon S \to X$, $x_v(\lambda s) = \lambda v$, is linear, and
$x_v(s) = v$. Now suppose $f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y$ satisfy $f_1 x = f_2 x$ for
all linear $x \colon S \to X$. Then for every $v \in X$,
$$
f_1(v) = f_1 x_v (s) = f_2 x_v (s) = f_2(v),
$$
so $f_1 = f_2$. (In fact linear maps $S \to X$ correspond bijectively to
vectors of $X$ via $x \mapsto x(s)$; this is the sense in which $S$ plays the
role of $\one$.)

*$S$ is also a coseparator.* Let $a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A$ be linear with
$a_0 \neq a_1$. Then there is $t \in T$ with $w := a_0(t) - a_1(t) \neq 0$.
Extend $\{w\}$ to a basis $\{w, e_2, \dots, e_n\}$ of $A$ and let
$\varphi \colon A \to S$ be the linear map with $\varphi(w) = s$ and
$\varphi(e_i) = 0$. Then
$$
\varphi a_0 (t) - \varphi a_1 (t) = \varphi(w) = s \neq 0,
$$
so $\varphi a_0 \neq \varphi a_1$. (We had to use generalized elements
$T \to A$ here, because maps out of the terminal object carry no information
in this category; see the next point.)

*The terminal object is not a separator.* The zero space $\{0\}$ is terminal:
from any $X$ there is exactly one linear map to it, the zero map. It is also
initial: the only linear map $\{0\} \to X$ sends $0 \mapsto 0$. So for any
$f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y$ and any $x \colon \{0\} \to X$, both $f_1 x$ and
$f_2 x$ are the unique map $\{0\} \to Y$, hence equal. Taking $f_1 = \id{S}$
and $f_2 = 0$ (distinct, since $s \neq 0$) shows that $\{0\}$ does not
separate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to (b): groups

*Category.* The identity map is a homomorphism. If $f \colon G \to H$ and
$g \colon H \to K$ are homomorphisms then
$gf(xy) = g(f(x)f(y)) = gf(x)\, gf(y)$.

*$(\Z, +)$ is a separator.* For each element $x$ of a group $X$ the map
$h_x \colon \Z \to X$, $h_x(n) = x^n$, is a homomorphism (since
$x^{m+n} = x^m x^n$) with $h_x(1) = x$. If $f_1, f_2 \colon X \to Y$ satisfy
$f_1 h = f_2 h$ for every homomorphism $h \colon \Z \to X$, then for every
$x \in X$,
$$
f_1(x) = f_1 h_x(1) = f_2 h_x(1) = f_2(x),
$$
so $f_1 = f_2$. (As in (a), homomorphisms $\Z \to X$ correspond bijectively to
elements of $X$, because $\Z$ is the free group on one generator.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to (c): partially ordered sets

*Category.* The identity is monotone. If $f, g$ are monotone and $x \le y$
then $f(x) \le f(y)$, hence $g f(x) \le g f(y)$.

*The terminal object is a separator.* The one-element poset
$\one = \{\ast\}$ is terminal (the constant map $X \to \one$ is monotone and
is the only map). Every function $\one \to X$ is monotone, so monotone maps
$\one \to X$ correspond exactly to points of $X$. If $f_1 x = f_2 x$ for all
$x \colon \one \to X$, then $f_1$ and $f_2$ agree at every point, so they are
equal as functions, hence as arrows. So, unlike (a) and (b), $\one$ is a
separator here.

*There is a coseparator: the two-element chain $\two = \{0 < 1\}$.* Let
$a_0, a_1 \colon T \to A$ be monotone with $a_0 \neq a_1$; pick $t$ with
$p := a_0(t) \neq q := a_1(t)$. By antisymmetry, $p \not\le q$ or
$q \not\le p$; say $p \not\le q$ (otherwise swap the roles of $p$ and $q$).
Define $\varphi \colon A \to \two$ by
$$
\varphi(z) =
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } p \le z,\\
  0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
$$
the indicator of the up-set ${\uparrow}p$. It is monotone: if $z \le z'$ and
$\varphi(z) = 1$ then $p \le z \le z'$, so $\varphi(z') = 1$. And
$\varphi(p) = 1 \neq 0 = \varphi(q)$ since $p \not\le q$. Hence
$\varphi a_0 (t) \neq \varphi a_1 (t)$, so $\varphi a_0 \neq \varphi a_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to (d): finite state machines

Objects are triples $(Q, \alpha, \beta)$ with $\alpha, \beta \colon Q \to Q$;
an arrow $(Q, \alpha, \beta) \to (Q', \alpha', \beta')$ is a mapping
$\varphi \colon Q \to Q'$ with $\varphi\alpha = \alpha'\varphi$ and
$\varphi\beta = \beta'\varphi$.

*Composition* is composition of the underlying mappings: given
$\varphi \colon (Q, \alpha, \beta) \to (Q', \alpha', \beta')$ and
$\psi \colon (Q', \alpha', \beta') \to (Q'', \alpha'', \beta'')$, set
$\psi \circ \varphi := \psi\varphi$. It is a homomorphism, by associativity in
$\Set$:
$$
(\psi\varphi)\alpha = \psi(\varphi\alpha) = \psi(\alpha'\varphi)
= (\psi\alpha')\varphi = (\alpha''\psi)\varphi = \alpha''(\psi\varphi),
$$
and the same computation with $\beta$ in place of $\alpha$.

*Identities:* $\id{Q}$ is a homomorphism
$(Q, \alpha, \beta) \to (Q, \alpha, \beta)$, since
$\id{Q}\alpha = \alpha = \alpha\,\id{Q}$, and likewise for $\beta$.

By the common remark above, associativity and the identity laws are inherited
from $\Set$, so machines and their homomorphisms form a category.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Remarks

- *Terminal = initial.* In vector spaces (and in groups) the zero space
  (trivial group) is both terminal and initial. So in these categories
  $\zero \cong \one$: the Nondegeneracy axiom *fails*. This is a good way to
  see why Nondegeneracy is a genuine axiom and not a triviality.
- *Separators replace $\one$.* In (a) and (b) the terminal object sees
  nothing, and a different object ($k$, respectively $\Z$) does the job of
  "detecting elements". In each case that object is the *free* structure on
  one generator, so maps out of it are the same as elements of the underlying
  set.
- *Groups have no coseparator.* If $C$ were one, take a simple group $G$ of
  cardinality larger than $C$ (alternating groups $A_n$, $n \ge 5$, give
  arbitrarily large finite examples). The kernel of any homomorphism
  $\varphi \colon G \to C$ is normal, hence trivial or all of $G$; it cannot
  be trivial for cardinality reasons, so $\varphi$ is trivial. Then no
  $\varphi$ distinguishes two different elements of $G$ (viewed as
  homomorphisms $\Z \to G$).
- *The order on the value object matters.* The *discrete* two-element poset
  (no order relations between its two points) is *not* a coseparator in
  posets: monotone maps into it are constant on connected components, so for
  instance the two elements of the chain $\two$ cannot be told apart by maps
  into it.
- *Finite dimension* is only used in (a) for the easy extension of $\{w\}$ to
  a basis; with the Axiom of Choice the same argument works for all vector
  spaces.
- *Machines* preview a later theme of the book (Chapter 10): many categories
  of structures are categories of "sets with endomaps". The terminal machine
  has one state with $\alpha = \beta = \mathrm{id}$, so elements
  $\one \to (Q, \alpha, \beta)$ are exactly the states fixed by both $\alpha$
  and $\beta$. Hence $\one$ is not a separator: for $Q = \{0, 1\}$ with
  $\alpha = \beta$ both equal to the swap there are no maps from $\one$ at all, but
  $\id{Q}$ and the swap are two distinct homomorphisms $Q \to Q$.
:::

## Which Chapter 1 axioms hold where?

The following table summarizes what @exr-LR-1-30 reveals. The axioms
"$\one$ separates mappings" and "$\zero \not\cong \one$" already rule out many
familiar categories of structures, though not all of them. (The machine row
goes slightly beyond the exercise; see the remarks above.)

| Category | terminal $\one$ | initial $\zero$ | $\zero \not\cong \one$ | $\one$ separates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sets $\Set$ | one-element set | empty set | yes | yes |
| Vector spaces | $\{0\}$ | $\{0\}$ | no | no |
| Groups | trivial group | trivial group | no | no |
| Posets | one-point poset | empty poset | yes | yes |
| Machines | one state, identities | empty machine | yes | no |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Question

Posets satisfy every axiom of Chapter 1. What distinguishes them from abstract
sets?
:::

In posets a monotone bijection need not be an isomorphism: the identity
function from the discrete two-element poset to the chain $\two$ is monotone
and bijective, but its inverse is not monotone. Such behaviour is ruled out by
the further axioms of the book, which make the category of abstract sets a
topos.
